design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (Review Manager 4.2.9; relative risks) of double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized trials of central nervous system stimulant medication for cocaine dependence. PubMed, the Cochrane Library and IDIS searched from 1966 to November 2006 (last search 1 December 2006), with reference lists and contact with first authors; the list of stimulant drugs was built from ATC and AHFS drug classes. Nine trials (640 patients, 11 drug-placebo comparisons) of mazindol (2), dexamphetamine (3), methylphenidate (2), modafinil (1) and bupropion (1). Outcomes: dropout, cocaine use as the proportion of urine samples positive for benzoylecgonine during the trial, craving (not pooled) and dropout for adverse events. A planned exploratory analysis added three trials whose cocaine use during the trial was imputed as the mean of the baseline and final proportions of positive urines.
can_establish: Whether, in the nine placebo-controlled trials published by 2006 (640 patients, mostly men, about half also opioid-dependent, mostly smoking or injecting cocaine), stimulant medications singly or together reduced dropout or the proportion of cocaine-positive urine samples, and how often they led to dropout for adverse events.
cannot_establish: Efficacy of any single drug with useful precision (one to three small trials each, 30 to 149 patients, 42 to 182 days); effects in women, in people who snort cocaine or in people without opioid dependence; effects beyond six months; the safety of these drugs beyond dropout for adverse events; or whether the exploratory signal for dexamphetamine is real, since it rests on imputed outcomes and on per-protocol data from two trials by one group.

sample.recruitment: Database search: PubMed, the Cochrane Library and the Iowa Drug Information System, each from 1966 to November 2006, run twice (last search 1 December 2006); reference lists of retrieved trials and four reviews hand-searched; first authors contacted for further articles (p. 1872, Search strategy). Fig. 2 also names clinicaltrials.gov among the databases. 584 citations screened (582 in the text), 551 excluded as not assessing a stimulant for cocaine dependence, 33 potentially eligible, 24 excluded (20 open trials, 2 pharmacokinetic trials, 2 crossover trials), 9 included; four trials were supplemented with unpublished data from their authors (p. 1873; Fig. 2, p. 1875).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled parallel-group trials of a stimulant in patients with cocaine dependence reporting retention, cocaine use by urine benzoylecgonine, or craving; no publication restrictions. Excluded: trials of people with cocaine abuse rather than dependence (p. 1872). Stimulants: drugs from selected ATC and AHFS classes with at least one published study showing a stimulant effect (pp. 1872-1873). From a report of two trials, only the dexamphetamine trial was used (p. 1875).
sample.demographics: Pooled baseline characteristics from the trials reporting each (Table 2, p. 1879): 11.9% women; mean age 34.9; 48.3% White, 40.9% Black, 10.8% other; 28.6% employed; mean years of cocaine use 7.7 to 14.0 across trials; 65.3% used crack; route intranasal 12.8%, smoked 51.4%, intravenous 35.8%; 46.9% opioid-dependent, 88.1% of whom were in the three trials requiring dual dependence; ADHD 7.6%. Adult ADHD was an inclusion criterion in one trial (Schubiner 2002), an exclusion criterion in three, and not assessed or not specified in five (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Dropout 167 of 344 on stimulants and 138 of 296 on placebo (48.5% and 46.6%, editors' arithmetic from Fig. 3, p. 1880). Cocaine use was analysed per protocol in the two Grabowski dexamphetamine trials (Table 1: 112 of 128 with at least one positive urine at baseline; an evaluable sample of 62 of 94 who took at least one dose) (pp. 1876-1877).
sample.selection_effects: Few, small trials; eight of nine funded by NIDA; mostly men who smoke or inject cocaine, about half also opioid-dependent and treated with methadone; every trial added psychotherapy of varying intensity (Table 1). The authors judge the pooled sample biased towards patients with a poor prognosis (p. 1882; p. 1884).

exposure.measurement: Randomized, double-blind assignment to drug or placebo within each trial.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Oral daily doses as given in the trials (Table 1, pp. 1876-1878): mazindol 1 mg or 2 mg; sustained-release dexamphetamine 15-30 or 30-60 mg (two trials, one with methadone 1.1 mg/kg/day in all arms) and immediate-release dexamphetamine 20-60 mg; immediate-release methylphenidate 30-90 mg, or 45 mg of immediate plus sustained release; modafinil 200-400 mg; bupropion 200-300 mg. Planned follow-up 42 to 182 days.
exposure.polysubstance: About half the patients were opioid-dependent; three trials required dual cocaine and opioid dependence with methadone maintenance. Some trials excluded dependence on other drugs and one did not (Table 1). Alcohol use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: cocaine use was the outcome, measured by urine benzoylecgonine once every 2 weeks to three times a week depending on the trial (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Placebo with the same psychotherapy as the drug arm in each trial; in the two three-arm trials the placebo group was divided between the two comparisons (p. 1873).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparisons; ADHD status unknown in five trials.

outcomes.instruments: Dropout (failure to complete the trial); cocaine use as the proportion of benzoylecgonine-positive urine samples during the trial; craving by a 0-10 Likert scale, visual analogue scales, a 5-point analogue scale, the Tiffany cocaine craving questionnaire, or the CSSA, BSCS and CCQ; dropout for adverse events; trial quality by the Jadad scale (0 to 5, below 3 poor), which rates the reporting of randomization, double-blinding and withdrawals (p. 1873; Table 3, p. 1882).
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine benzoylecgonine is objective; craving instruments differ between trials, so craving was not pooled.
outcomes.operationalization: Cocaine use RR: ratio of the proportions of positive urine samples, entered in Fig. 4 as events out of the number of patients (for example 17/30 vs 25/32 for modafinil), so the proportion of samples is treated as if it were a proportion of patients; the authors say these data were transformed to fit the other pooled studies (p. 1880).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcome families; editors' count of 21 pooled estimates in Figs 3 and 4 (five drugs and two totals for each of dropout, main and exploratory cocaine use), plus two post hoc subgroup estimates and the adverse-event comparison.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: All trials double-blind (an inclusion criterion); blinding integrity was not assessed. In the review, one author selected trials and extracted data, a second checked the extraction, and reviewers were not blinded to authorship or journal (p. 1873).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects relative risks (drug vs placebo). Dropout (Fig. 3, p. 1880): mazindol 0.93 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.47); dexamphetamine 0.90 (0.71 to 1.12), I-squared 45.2%; methylphenidate 1.15 (0.77 to 1.73); modafinil 1.07 (0.55 to 2.09); bupropion 0.86 (0.41 to 1.79); all stimulants without bupropion 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); all 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10), I-squared 0%. Cocaine-positive urines, main analysis of six trials (Fig. 4A, p. 1881): mazindol 0.53 (0.11 to 2.54); dexamphetamine 0.81 (0.56 to 1.16); methylphenidate 1.09 (0.72 to 1.64); modafinil 0.73 (0.50 to 1.04), p = 0.08; bupropion 0.98 (0.86 to 1.12); all without bupropion 0.84 (0.67 to 1.04); all 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05). Exploratory analysis of nine trials with imputed values (Fig. 4B): dexamphetamine 0.73 (0.60 to 0.90), p = 0.003; all without bupropion 0.82 (0.71 to 0.94); all 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99), p = 0.03. Post hoc, trials requiring dual cocaine and opioid dependence: dropout 0.85 (0.56 to 1.30), cocaine use 0.86 (0.68 to 1.09) (p. 1879). Dropout for adverse events 15/344 (4.4%) vs 4/296 (1.3%), p = 0.03 (p. 1879). No absolute risk differences or prediction intervals. Editors' checks: DerSimonian-Laird pooling of the printed counts reproduces the dropout totals and every Fig. 4 total; from the same counts, retention gives RR 1.03 (0.93 to 1.15), not the abstract's 0.94; without the high-dose arm of Grabowski 2001 the exploratory dexamphetamine RR becomes 0.79 (0.62 to 1.00).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (randomized comparisons). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, a subanalysis by Jadad score (results described in one sentence) and a post hoc subanalysis of dual-dependence trials.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Analyses by drug and for all stimulants, and subanalyses by trial quality and ADHD, are described as planned a priori (pp. 1872-1873), but no registered or published protocol is cited; the analysis without bupropion and the dual-dependence subanalysis were post hoc (pp. 1873, 1879); the ADHD subanalysis could not be done.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's headline RRs for retention and cocaine use appear nowhere in the results; the Jadad-score subanalysis is reported without estimates; Table 3 gives no craving values for two trials; the abstract's statement that no serious adverse event was reported has no counterpart in the Results, and several trials did not specify adverse-event assessment (Table 1).
analysis.power: The authors calculate that 144 to 584 patients per arm (80% power, two-tailed p = 0.05, 50% dropout) would be needed, more than in any included trial (p. 1882).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across nine small trials (640 patients), no stimulant medication, singly or pooled, reduced dropout (all stimulants RR 0.97, 0.85 to 1.10) or cocaine-positive urines in the main analysis (all 0.94, 0.84 to 1.05; without bupropion 0.84, 0.67 to 1.04). Only an exploratory analysis that imputed cocaine use for three trials and used per-protocol data for two dexamphetamine trials showed fewer positive urines with dexamphetamine (0.73, 0.60 to 0.90) and with stimulants pooled (0.87, 0.77 to 0.99). Dropout for adverse events was 4.4% vs 1.3%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's main conclusion matches the results: the main outcomes do not support stimulants for cocaine dependence (p. 1871). But its two headline RRs (retention 0.94, 0.81 to 1.09; cocaine use 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02) are not in the figures, and it describes the secondary results as hopeful, mainly with dexamphetamine and modafinil. The modafinil estimate was not significant (0.73, 0.50 to 1.04); the dexamphetamine signal depends on means of baseline and final proportions, on per-protocol subsets of two trials by one group, and in part on one arm listed in Fig. 3 with 42 dropouts of 46; the Discussion calls per-protocol bias unlikely without analysis (p. 1884). The abstract's statement that no serious adverse event was reported is not supported by any result in the text, which describes information on adverse reactions as too limited to draw conclusions (p. 1880). The Discussion also reverses the exploratory reductions for all stimulants with and without bupropion (p. 1882).

timeline.event: Margolin et al. (mazindol; bupropion, two trials) and Stine et al. (mazindol): included trials, none showing differences in dropout, cocaine use or craving (Table 1).
Grabowski et al.: sustained-release dexamphetamine, cocaine use lower in the per-protocol sample; included (Table 1); its high-dose arm gives the largest exploratory effect in Fig. 4B.
Grabowski et al.: dexamphetamine with methadone in people with heroin dependence, cocaine use lower in the evaluable sample; included (Table 1).
Dackis et al.: modafinil, cocaine use lower in the trial's own analysis, a trend after the review's transformation; included (Table 1; p. 1880).
This meta-analysis; the authors call for a follow-up meta-analysis including the ongoing trials (p. 1884).
Pérez-Mañá et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of indirect dopamine agonists for psychostimulant dependence; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).
Sangroula et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of modafinil for cocaine dependence; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).
Biso et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of methylphenidate for cocaine use disorder; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).
Paterson et al.: systematic review of pharmacological interventions for cocaine use disorder; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).

replication.where_it_stands: An early meta-analysis of stimulant (agonist-like) medication for cocaine dependence covering nine trials to 2006. It supports only the statement that this evidence showed no benefit on dropout or on the main cocaine-use outcome; later reviews on the project's list must be appraised before the encyclopedia states where the question stands now.

funding.funder: Two grants to X. Castells, from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III (a public research body of the Spanish Ministry of Health) and from Mutual Mèdica de Catalunya i Balears (a mutual insurance company providing health insurance for physicians) (p. 1884, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of competing interests appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Psychiatry Service and Clinical Pharmacology Service (Fundació Institut Català de Farmacologia), Hospital Universitari Vall d'Hebron, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona. Of the included trials, eight of nine were NIDA-funded, three were co-funded by manufacturers (Wyeth for the two mazindol trials, Cephalon for modafinil) and one had pharmaceutical industry help (Table 1).

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered, registered, double-blind trials of single stimulant medications (particularly sustained-release dexamphetamine and modafinil) in people with cocaine use disorder, analysed by intention to treat with patient-level abstinence outcomes (for example urine-confirmed abstinent weeks), explicit handling of missing urines, checks of blinding, and inclusion of women and of people who neither inject nor use opioids; then an updated meta-analysis, ideally of individual patient data.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Patients with cocaine dependence, stimulant medication, placebo, retention, urine-confirmed cocaine use and craving (p. 1872).
Analyses are described as planned a priori, but no protocol is cited; two analyses were added post hoc.
Only double-blind parallel-group randomized trials were included, without stated reasons; open and crossover trials were excluded at the last step without explanation (Fig. 2).

Three databases with the PubMed strategy printed (Fig. 1), no publication restrictions, reference lists, contact with first authors and a search a month before submission; no Embase or PsycINFO and no grey literature; clinicaltrials.gov appears only in Fig. 2.
One author extracted with a standardized form and a second checked, with discrepancies resolved by consensus (p. 1873).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 24 trials excluded after full assessment appear only as category counts in Fig. 2.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives participants, design, randomization, drug and daily dose, psychotherapy, outcome measures, follow-up length, analysis type, funding and Jadad score for each trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The Jadad scale rates the reporting of randomization, blinding and withdrawals; it does not assess allocation concealment or selective reporting, and the authors themselves call it a reporting-quality scale (p. 1873).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding of each trial is in Table 1, summarized in the text (p. 1875).

Random-effects relative risks with split control groups are appropriate for dropout, but the cocaine-use outcome treats each group's proportion of positive urine samples as if it were a proportion of patients, the exploratory analysis imputes the outcome from baseline and final values, and per-protocol results are pooled with intention-to-treat results; the authors acknowledge the transformation (p. 1880). A close call for an outcome-level problem, recorded with the reasons.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The only analysis by trial quality used the Jadad score and is reported in one sentence without estimates (p. 1879).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Per-protocol bias in the two dexamphetamine trials is called unlikely without analysis (p. 1884); attrition of about 48%, unblinding by stimulant effects and selective reporting are not discussed, while the exploratory positive results are presented as hopeful.

Chi-square tests and I-squared reported for every pool; differences between the dexamphetamine trials are discussed (formulation, schedule, per-protocol analysis, a highly marginalized sample) (p. 1883).
Not investigated; the authors state it was controlled by searching several sources and contacting authors (p. 1883).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding is reported in the Acknowledgements, but there is no declaration of competing interests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence: six critical items are not met (no protocol, no list of excluded trials, a reporting-quality scale instead of a risk-of-bias assessment, an outcome transformation that treats urine samples as patients, no discussion of attrition or unblinding as sources of bias, no investigation of publication bias) and the search is only partly comprehensive. The null main results can still be cited because they are reproducible from the printed counts and consistent across drugs: dropout 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10) and positive urines 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05). The positive exploratory results cannot. Cite for: no detectable benefit of stimulant medications, singly or together, on dropout or on the proportion of cocaine-positive urines in the nine trials published by 2006 (640 patients, mostly men, about half opioid-dependent), and slightly more dropout for adverse events (4.4% vs 1.3%). Do not cite for: efficacy of dexamphetamine or modafinil, or the absence of serious harms.

key_findings.finding: Nine randomized trials met the criteria, with 640 patients (344 given a stimulant, 296 placebo) and 11 drug-placebo comparisons: mazindol 2 trials, dexamphetamine 3, methylphenidate 2, modafinil 1, bupropion 1; four trials were supplemented with unpublished author data.
key_findings.locator: Results › Article search, 1st paragraph (p. 1873) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1875); Fig. 2 (p. 1875)

key_findings.finding: Trials had 30 to 149 patients and 42 to 182 days of planned follow-up; seven were two-armed and two three-armed; eight of nine were funded by NIDA; Jadad scores were 2 (two trials), 3 (six) and 4 (one).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical trial and subject features, 1st paragraph (p. 1875); Table 1 (pp. 1876-1878)

key_findings.finding: Patients (Table 2): 11.9% women, mean age 34.9, 28.6% employed, 65.3% used crack, routes intranasal 12.8%, smoked 51.4% and intravenous 35.8%, 46.9% opioid-dependent (88.1% of them in three trials requiring dual dependence), ADHD 7.6%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Clinical trial and subject features, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text gives 89.1% men and 65.8% crack, against 11.9% women and 65.3% crack in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Dropout did not differ between stimulants and placebo for any drug or overall: all stimulants RR 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10), I-squared 0%; without bupropion 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); dexamphetamine 0.90 (0.71 to 1.12); methylphenidate 1.15 (0.77 to 1.73); modafinil 1.07 (0.55 to 2.09); mazindol 0.93 (0.59 to 1.47); bupropion 0.86 (0.41 to 1.79). Dropouts were 167 of 344 vs 138 of 296.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy and safety, 1st paragraph (p. 1879); Fig. 3 (p. 1880)

key_findings.finding: Main analysis of cocaine-positive urines (six trials): all stimulants RR 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05); without bupropion 0.84 (0.67 to 1.04); modafinil 0.73 (0.50 to 1.04), p = 0.08; dexamphetamine 0.81 (0.56 to 1.16); methylphenidate 1.09 (0.72 to 1.64); mazindol 0.53 (0.11 to 2.54); bupropion 0.98 (0.86 to 1.12). Leaving out each comparison in turn changed no conclusion.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy and safety, 1st paragraph (p. 1879); Fig. 4A (p. 1881)

key_findings.finding: Exploratory analysis adding three trials with cocaine use imputed as the mean of baseline and final proportions: dexamphetamine RR 0.73 (0.60 to 0.90), p = 0.003; all stimulants 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99), p = 0.03; without bupropion 0.82 (0.71 to 0.94).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data synthesis and statistical analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 1873); Results › Efficacy and safety, 2nd paragraph (p. 1879); Fig. 4B (p. 1881)
key_findings.note: The largest single contribution is the high-dose arm of Grabowski 2001 (0.60, 0.41 to 0.88; 31 patients analysed), an arm listed in Fig. 3 with 42 dropouts of 46; without it the dexamphetamine RR is 0.79 (0.62 to 1.00) (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Craving was not pooled because of different instruments; only one trial, of immediate-release dexamphetamine, found less craving (visual analogue scale 77 to 51 vs 77 to 67 with placebo, p < 0.01); the others found no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy and safety, 3rd paragraph (p. 1879); Table 3 (p. 1882)

key_findings.finding: Dropout for adverse events was higher with stimulants: 15 of 344 (4.4%) vs 4 of 296 (1.3%), p = 0.03; the commonest adverse events were sleeping problems, anxiety and jitteriness; no trial reported abuse of the study medication.

A post hoc subanalysis of the three trials requiring dual cocaine and opioid dependence gave RR 0.85 (0.56 to 1.30) for dropout and 0.86 (0.68 to 1.09) for cocaine use; trials with Jadad scores of 3 or more did not differ from those scoring below 3 (no estimates given); the planned ADHD subanalysis was impossible because only one trial reported it.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy and safety, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors calculate that 144 to 584 patients per arm (80% power, two-tailed p = 0.05, 50% dropout) would be needed, more than in any included trial, and suggest that lack of power, concomitant psychotherapy and poor-prognosis samples may have hidden efficacy.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives RR 0.94 (0.81 to 1.09) for retention and 0.90 (0.79 to 1.02) for cocaine use, but neither appears in the Results: Fig. 3 gives 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10) for dropout, and Fig. 4A gives 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05) with bupropion and 0.84 (0.67 to 1.04) without. Retention pooled from the Fig. 3 counts gives 1.03 (0.93 to 1.15) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's headline figures should not be cited; the figure values are reproducible from the printed counts and should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 3 lists Grabowski 2004-1 twice (the second row should be 2004-2), prints the Schubiner RR as 1.04 with CI 0.60 to 1.00 (from its counts, 0.60 to 1.80; editors' calculation) and the methylphenidate subtotal weight as 111.27 (the weights sum to 100 with 11.27).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting errors; the pooled results are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Trial sizes disagree between Table 1 and the forest plots: Grabowski 1997 is 49 in Table 1, 48 in Fig. 3 and 49 in Fig. 4; Schubiner 2002 is 48 in Table 1 and 49 in Figs 3 and 4; for Grabowski 2004 Table 1 gives an ITT sample of 94 but computes the evaluable share as 62/84 = 73.8% (62/94 = 66.0%); Grabowski 2001 contributes 100 patients to Fig. 4B against a per-protocol sample of 112 in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which patients entered each analysis cannot be fully reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 11.9% women and 65.3% crack, while the text gives 89.1% men and 65.8% crack.

Craving counts disagree: Fig. 2 lists 4 trials with usable craving data, the text says five trials used four instruments, and Table 3 lists six trials (two without data) with at least five instruments; the craving scale for Margolin 1995 [39] is a visual analogue scale in Table 1 and a 0-10 Likert scale in Table 3; Stine's craving measure is a 5-point scale but its means are 13.0 at baseline.
reporting_issues.consequence: The craving evidence is poorly specified; the single positive craving result (Shearer 2003) is not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the exploratory analysis showed a 13% or 18% reduction with all stimulants without or with bupropion, respectively, while Fig. 4B gives 0.82 (an 18% reduction) without bupropion and 0.87 (13%) with it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two figures are reversed in the Discussion.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion attributes Grabowski's positive results to withdrawing those who dropped out [42] or those who never gave a positive urine [45], while Table 1 describes the per-protocol rule of [42] as at least one positive urine at baseline and that of [45] as having taken at least one dose.
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis of the per-protocol samples, on which the dexamphetamine signal depends, is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation and wording errors: Table 3 cites Schubiner 2002 as [44] (Shearer's number; Schubiner is [43]); the Table 1 caption cites the Jadad scale as [33] (it is [35]); the two-armed trials are cited as [37-41,43,44], where [37] is a methods reference and Dackis [46] is missing; the text says sample sizes ranged from 30 to 149 days; Table 1 describes the Grabowski 2004 participants as cocaine- and methadone-naive heroin-dependent patients, which taken literally contradicts their inclusion; 582 citations in the text against 584 in Fig. 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor errors that make the review harder to audit.
